find_compound.description: Turn whatever names a chemical into the chemical itself. Give a name, a brand, a CAS number, a structure drawn as SMILES or InChI, an InChI key, a molecular formula or a PubChem CID, and get back the formula, the weight, the structure as text, the properties that decide how a molecule behaves, and a plain language description of what it actually is. This is the step to put first: everything else here takes the same kinds of value, so once a spreadsheet column or a form answer has been run through this, the rest of the workflow knows exactly which molecule it is dealing with.

find_similar_compounds.description: Find the molecules that look like one you already have. PubChem compares the structures themselves rather than their names, so this surfaces the analogue nobody thought to name similarly: a generic beside a brand, a metabolite beside its parent, a cheaper reagent beside an expensive one. Set how alike they have to be, from 50 for a loose family resemblance to 95 and above for near twins. The compound you asked about always comes back first and is flagged, so a workflow can drop it in one step.

get_assay.description: Read one biological experiment in full: what it set out to measure, the protein or organism it was aimed at, how it was run, how many compounds went through it and how many came out active, and which those were. The description and protocol are the researchers' own words, so this is where a result stops being a number and becomes something you can judge. Assay numbers come from 'List a compound's test results' or from looking up a gene.

get_compound_details.description: Build one table of chemistry across a whole list of compounds. Hand it the column out of a spreadsheet, a form or an earlier step, up to a hundred at a time, tick the facts you want, and get a row per compound with those columns filled in. Anything PubChem cannot place comes back in its own list rather than being quietly dropped, so a run over real data says exactly which rows need a human. list_compound_activity.description: Read what a chemical has actually been tested against and what each experiment concluded. PubChem holds over a million biological assays, and a widely studied compound appears in thousands of them: this returns a row per result with the experiment, the verdict, the protein it was tested against and the potency where one was measured, plus a tally of how the verdicts break down. Filter to the active results to see only where something worked, which is how to tell a molecule with a real biological story from one that has simply been screened a lot.

list_compound_references.description: Find out who has written about a chemical and who holds it. Returns the papers that mention it, linked straight to PubMed; the patents that claim it, linked to Google Patents; the databases and suppliers that carry a record for it, with links back to those records; and the catalogue numbers they file it under. Use it to gauge how well studied something is before committing to it, to watch a competitor's patent activity, or to find where else to buy a reagent. search_by_structure.description: Search a hundred million compounds by shape rather than by name. Draw a fragment and ask what contains it, to find every molecule built around a particular ring or group. Or name a whole molecule and ask what it is part of, to find the salts, esters and mixtures it turns up in. Or ask for the exact structure, which is how to check whether something has already been catalogued. Or ask for everything sharing a molecular formula, which is how to find the isomers that weigh the same and behave differently.

description: Look up any chemical from a workflow. PubChem is the world's largest open chemistry database, run by the US National Library of Medicine: around 120 million compounds, their properties, their names, the papers and patents that mention them, and 1.7 million biological experiments testing what they do. Turn a column of chemical names, brands or CAS numbers into formulas, weights, structures and drug likeness figures. Search a hundred million structures by what they contain rather than what they are called, or find the molecules that look like one you already have. Read what a compound has been tested against and what happened, or start from a gene and find the chemistry aimed at it. Download the structure as a file for modelling software, or as a clean drawing for a report. Every action takes whatever names a chemical, from a brand name to a SMILES string, and works out which it is. No account or API key required.
